rv.q: Crucially, whether bickering about art or madly wielding golf clubs, the leads spark off each other, often to hair-raising effect.
They’re both giving the finest stage performances of their careers to date, but you get the sense that they’re both having enormous fun too.
It’s a nicely conceived, sharply executed vision of the play.

Come the arrival of Madeleine Potter’s affectless Mom, surveying an attempted strangulation, hands in pockets, as if she was noticing a speck on the carpet, it’s pretty much perfect in its peculiarity.
I’ve seen more visceral and menacing accounts of this play, but here you get an engaging dose of its visceral elation.
But as envy comes into the open – the one wanting intellect, the other action – and warfare breaks out, Matthew Dunster’s production loses power.
But, enjoyable as Matthew Dunster’s revival is, I felt the play works best in small theatres and that the central pairing doesn’t achieve a perfect balance.
But Matthew Dunster’s production sells it a bit short.

But the result is a disaster, one of the worst acted and least convincing productions of any Shepard play that I have ever seen, one that reduces a resonant masterwork to an incomprehensible screaming match.
I couldn’t wait to escape this opaque, witless and dementedly pessimistic horror show.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this West End revival of Shepard's sibling rivalry drama, with praise for Harington and Flynn's performances but questions about whether the play works in a larger venue. Some find it darkly funny and sharp; others call it gloomy and flawed.
